div.p: One important requirement of many real-time systems is the ability to undergo several mutually exclusive modes of operation. By means of a mode change the system changes its functionality over time, thus being able to adapt to changing environmental situations. In order to successfully include mode changes in real-time systems, a mode change protocol with well known real-time behaviour is necessary. In this paper we provide a new model and related schedulability analysis for mode changes in flexible real-time systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: One way to cope with dynamically changing functional and performance requirements in real-time systems is to introduce in the system's architecture mode change protocols. These will allow more flexible systems, which are able to migrate from one mode to another in a controlled manner. A mode change protocol should be able to correctly schedule the system's tasks during the mode change window. The ability to timely introduce new tasks and delete old versions while scheduling unmodified real-time tasks across a mode change window is therefore an important element of design in modern real-time systems.

A more comprehensive discussion of the issues of realtime system design and operation affected by different modes and changes between them can be found in [5]. In this paper we discuss the schedulability of mode changes in flexible real-time systems.

A system that is schedulable both in an old mode of operation and in a new mode of operation is not necessarily schedulable during the mode change. During a mode change new tasks can be introduced or old ones can be deleted. The task set is therefore altered, and because old and new tasks mutually interfere, we need a specific analysis to verify whether tasks during a mode change are schedulable.

This paper is structured as follows: the mode change model used to represent mode changes is examined in section 2. In section 3 we briefly review previous work on mode changes. The related schedulability analysis is presented in section 4. Additionally, a numerical example illustrating the applicability of the analysis is given in section 5. Finally, we present the discussions and the conclusion in sections 6 and 7 respectively.

div.head: The mode change model
div.p: The mode change model is based on the following assumptions:
Tasks are assigned fixed priorities by the Deadline Monotonic Scheduling algorithm (DMS) and executed in a uniprocessor system.
Tasks are not permitted to voluntarily suspend themselves during an invocation (so, for example, tasks are not allowed to execute internal Ada-like delay statements).
There are fixed task sets before and after the mode change.
The worst-case response time of a generic task i (W-CRT), denoted R i , is the longest time ever taken by that i from the time it arrives until the time it completes its required computation.

Tasks are scheduled with time offsets during the mode change only. This time phasing between tasks may or may not hold after the mode change. 2)) guarantees the schedulability of tasks in the steady state. Given the current mode, a mode change request and a set of tasks, our goal is to find out whether tasks are schedulable across the mode change. Inherent to the schedulability analysis is the fact that old tasks that advance through the mode change period in order to complete, interfere and suffer interference from new tasks released in the mode change.
We shall consider a set of periodic or sporadic tasks = f 1 ; 2 ; ::: i ; :: p g. Each task i is characterized by the tuple S i = fT i ; D i ; C i ; P i g, where:
T i and D i are respectively the period of task i (or, if a sporadic task, the minimum inter-arrival time between successive tasks of the stream i) and the deadline (latest ending time).
C i is the worst case execution time of the task i. This value is deemed to contain the overheads due to context switching. Moreover, the values of C i , D i and T i are such that C i D i T i .
P i represents the priority of task i, assigned according to the Deadline Monotonic Scheduling algorithm.
The proposed mode change protocol defines five classes of tasks as illustrated in figure 1 (solid lines):

Old mode completed version ( iO ): the old task set represents the functionality that the system delivers before the mode change. These tasks are therefore released prior to the arrival of a mode change request in the system, but their execution may span the whole duration of a mode change, provided only that deadlines are not missed. Tasks belonging to this class that are under execution when the mode change request arrives are allowed to complete during the mode change. From the application point of view, the completed task set is useful to represent the functionality that has safety-critical implications to the system. The system executes the mode change while also delivering the old functionality in order to leave the system in a safe condition. Also, tasks that have started need to finish for data consistency and future executions. Subsection 4.1 introduces the analysis for old mode version tasks across a mode change.

Old mode aborted version ( iA ): aborted tasks are immediately abandoned at the time a mode change request arrives and is accepted by the system. Their execution time is confined exclusively in the old mode, ie. do not execute during the mode change. From the application point of view, the functionality provided by this class of tasks is no longer necessary at the start of a mode change and thus can be discarded. For the sake of the system's real-time performance, they need to be quickly eliminated in order to reduce interference over the remaining tasks.

Wholly new mode version iW : wholly new tasks represent new added functionality to the system, ie. unlike other new mode tasks, they do not change or replace any old mode version task. Furthermore, they can be introduced in the system with an offset Y i anytime later than the mode change request (ie. Y i 0).

From the application point of view this class of tasks not only provides the system with a new functionality but it also caters for situations where it is required to introduce tasks as soon as the mode change request occurs, as may be the case of more critical tasks. The schedulability of wholly new tasks also need to be guaranteed while they are executing in the mode transition. The related analysis is discussed in subsection 4.2.

Changed new and Unchanged new tasks ( iC , iU ): this class of tasks implement the system's changed and unchanged functionality respectively. Each task in this class is always preceded by a corresponding old mode task i,1O (tasks in doted lines in figure 1) with com- putational time and period that may be changed during the mode change. Changed and unchanged new tasks can be introduced with an offset Y i any time later than the end of the period of the last release of the preceding old mode version. This condition may be necessary to allow the corresponding old mode task to complete. Both types need to be guaranteed across the mode change. We further refer to changed and unchanged tasks in section 4.

A mode change request M i is essentially a sporadic event that can only be serviced if the system is running in the steady state, ie. we must allow the system to terminate a mode change in order to be able to undergo a subsequent mode change. We also define the latency of a mode change R mc by a 'window starting with the arrival of the mode change request to the system and ending when the set of new tasks have completed their first execution and the set of old tasks have completed their last execution'.

The worst case latency of a mode change R mc occurs when all old mode tasks are released at the start of the mode change in a critical instant. It is given by the largest WCRT of a task in the mode change window ( taking into account the offset Y i for new tasks):
div.formula: R mc = max R iO , x; Y i + R iN 8 i (1)
div.p: where: R iO and R iN are the WCRT of the old mode task i and the WCRT of the new mode task i respectively, both given in section 4; x is the time at which the mode change arrives at the system, counted from the release of the old mode task i (subsection 4.1).

Whenever necessary, we use the notation C iO , C iA and C iN when referring (for example) to the computational time of a generic old, aborted and new task i respectively. The same idea applies to the other parameters and other types of tasks. Throughout the rest of the paper i denotes a task for which we are finding the worstcase response time and j denotes a higher priority task. We also use hp iO , hp iA , hp iN to represent the set of old, aborted and new tasks (respectively) with higher priority than task i.

div.head: Previous work
div.p: Mode changes have been handled in current industrial practice according to static cyclic schedules [10]. The so called major period is given by the least common multiple of the task periods. Mode changes are performed at the end of the major period of the old schedule. If that period is long, then the mode change is consequently delayed for a long time. One way of minimising such delays is to introduce fixed priority preemptive scheduling with deadline monotonic and rate monotonic analysis [3] [4] [9]. On account of the fact that new tasks can potentially be released without the need to wait for the end of a scheduling cycle, these techniques provide faster and more flexible mode changes. Another important drawback of previous works on mode changes has been the fact that mode changes have traditionally been modeled as an instantaneous event, taking no time to accomplish. This is clearly an assumption that needs to be removed if we want to address more realistic systems and applications. Additionally, the system can benefit in terms of flexibility by having a mode change that is carried out in a time window.

Sha et al [12] attempt to address the problem of analysing a priori a single processor system, scheduled according to the rate monotonic scheduling policy, with tasks able to lock and unlock semaphores according to the priority ceiling protocol. The mode change protocol they propose is a simple one, where tasks are either deleted or added across a mode change. An 'on the fly' record of the processor utilization is kept, and a task is added if the resulting task set is schedulable according to the exact-case rate monotonic scheduling equations [8]. The utilization of an old task can be 'reclaimed' at the end of the period of the old task. Furthermore, the behaviour of the tasks under the priority ceiling protocol is addressed by a set of rules that specify when semaphore ceilings can be raised and lowered, and when new tasks locking semaphores can be added to the system. However, the protocol and analysis have some disadvantages:

The analysis is not sufficient (i.e. the test may pass a task set that is unschedulable). The analysis was subsequently found to be faulty [13] because of the reliance on a view that utilisation is the key aspect of real-time scheduling.

The algorithm is confined to single processors. Although the priority inheritance protocol has been extended to multiprocessor cases [11] its application to distributed systems is severely restricted. The non neglectable communication delays and the induced overheads for the handling of global semaphores impose intractable run-time costs.

The supported task model is, however, limited to the use of semaphores as synchronization structure, and to tasks with deadlines which are equal to their periods. Thus, the application of the algorithm to systems requiring complex task dependencies and end-to-end deadlines on task groups is prevented.

The work of Tindell et al [13] propose a hard real-time computational model and a mode change protocol for single processor systems extending the deadline monotonic framework [7], in a similar way that the above discussed method extends the rate monotonic [4] and semaphore based scheduling models to mode changes. A schedulability test is presented for simple mode changes. The analysis presented provides new sufficient analysis. The analysis is also extended to allow tasks to lock semaphores. The main difference to the algorithm of [12] is the possibility to set deadlines of tasks to values smaller than their periods. However, the same limitations apply, and in addition no multiprocessor version has been presented.

In [6] mode changes are performed by switching from one static schedule to another. When a mode change is requested, it is checked if a switch to the transition schedule is feasible. Once the switch to a transition schedule has been carried out, it is executed so that all of its activities are completed once. Then a switch to the destination mode schedule is performed, which then executes periodically until another mode change is requested.

The work presented in this paper is based in the work of Tindell et al [13]. In the proposed model the introduction of a new task to the system always occurs immediately after the end of the period of the related old task. The schedulability analysis is needed to guarantee that tasks do not miss their deadlines while in the mode change.

In this work we adopt a slightly different approach: a new task can be released with an offset from the start of the mode change, at any time later than the period of the corresponding old mode task. Because offsets can be made large enough so that old and new tasks do not interfere (or their interference is minimal), the schedulability of the system is always feasible. Therefore our concern is instead to find the minimum duration for a mode change that still holds the schedulability property. This involves the selection of appropriate offsets for the new task set so that the mode change time is minimal. In this paper we present the model and its schedulability analysis -the work on the minimization of a mode change is the subject of current research.

div.head: Schedulability analysis
div.p: In this section we derive the worst-case response time analysis for the proposed mode change model. The analysis for the old and the new mode tasks is considered separately. We are interested solely in the WCRT of tasks during a mode change, where the schedulability condition must be guaranteed. We thus neglect from now on all steady state response times.

As we have seen in section 2 wholly new tasks, changed tasks and unchanged tasks belong to the same major class of new tasks. The way each new task interferes and is affected by a mode change is similar. Consequently, as we shall see in the next subsections, their timing analysis is the samefrom the scheduling analysis point of view these tasks share the same WCRT equations, the only difference between them being the values assigned to their minimum offset (Y iWmin = 0 and Y iCmin = Y iUmin = T i,1O ).
Therefore, for the sake of the simplicity of the analysis they will henceforth be referred to simply as 'new mode tasks' and denoted by N .

A changed new task iC is represented in the analysis with different period and/or computational time in relation to the corresponding parameters of the old mode completed version (ie. T iC 6 = T i,1O and/or C iC 6 = C i,1O ), while an unchanged task iU maintains the same values of T i and C i of the preceding old mode task. Furthermore, we can think in terms of the analysis that wholly new tasks are preceded by a 'null' old mode task (ie. C i,1O = 0 ).

div.p: Because new mode tasks suffer from interference from other higher priority new and other higher priority old tasks, we need to guarantee their schedulability during the mode change. div.head: WCRT analysis example
div.p: In this section we show a simplified example of the applicability of the analysis. The goal is to verify the schedulability of a task set according to the equations derived in the previous section. The task set is composed of old completed ( 1O and 5O ), changed ( 2C ), aborted ( 3A ), wholly new ( 4W ) and unchanged ( 6U ) tasks. The latency of the mode change is also checked according to the new analysis derived (equation ( 1)). It is determined by task 6U (ie. R mc = 300 ms). The set of values of x over which to apply equation 10 are x 0; 90. The significant values are 1, 20 and 61 ms (ie. 1; C 3A ; T 1O + ). The value of x that gives the WCRT for task 5O is x = 6 1 ms.

The schedulability of the above task set is assessed as follows: task 1O is unaffected by the mode change, since it is the highest priority task. Therefore static analysis (equation 2) is used to evaluate the WCRT; task 2C has the minimum offset that guarantees the schedulability of the system. Any offset less than 90 ms causes task 5O to miss its deadline. In other words, if task 2C is introduced immediately after the period of the old mode task 1O , 5O misses its deadline. Therefore by stretching the period of old mode task 1O in the mode change by 30 ms task 5O becomes schedulable. The WCRT of aborted task 3A in the old mode is evaluated according to the static deadline monotonic analysis (R 3A = 4 0 ms). However, we clearly do not need to guarantee the WCRT of an abortable task at the mode change; task 4W does not affect the schedulability of the mode change, and it can be introduced immediately at the start of the mode change (ie. Y 4 = 0); task 5O has the schedulability guaranteed by delaying the new task 2C . It is also possible to delay the introduction of 4W so that task 5C is schedulable; task 6U can only be introduced with an offset larger than or equal to 200 ms (T 5O = 200 ms). It executes in the steady-state since all old mode tasks have completed before its introduction, and therefore it is likewise evaluated according to equation 2.
As the value of the worst case response time of each task is less than the deadline, the system is deemed to be schedulable.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: In [13], new mode tasks have to be released immediately at the end of the period of the corresponding old mode task. One key point in this work is therefore the fact that we remove this restriction by introducing offsets to new mode tasks across a mode change. This offsets can be seen as a 'period-stretching' whereby the last release of an old mode task has its period increased (by Y i , T i,1O at least), thus allowing new mode tasks to be released at any time later than the period of the old mode task. All new tasks crossing a mode change may have a time-phasing specified by the different values of Y i for each task, which is guaranteed to exist during the mode change. It is not our concern in this work if this phasing is continued in the new mode. Whereas new tasks can have an arbitrarily large value for the offset, it may be desirable to limit these values for a number of tasks, in order to keep the granularity of the system. One possibility is to bound the offset to a maximum value such as T i,1O Y i T i,1O + T iN , which is large enough to allow the old mode task to complete in the mode change and let the new version to start thereafter.

Offsets in real-time systems can be used for a number of purposes. An important observation is that the selection of offsets is a flexible requirement in nature, ie. provided that the system meets its overall requirements the actual value of an offset does not matter. We can thus take advantage of this flexibility -it is possible by choosing appropriate offsets to increase the schedulability of a mode change. If there is an overload at the start of a mode change, where the utilization may increase above the limit, the system may be deemed unschedulable. By means of offsets, the new task set can be delayed from the start of a mode change and spread across it so that the interference that new tasks experience from higher priority old mode tasks (and vice versa) is reduced, thus allowing tasks sets to complete before their deadlines. This also allows to reduce the pessimism in the timing analysis due to the critical interval potentially generated at the start of the mode change.

Another possibility is to use offsets to minimize the duration of a mode change. Because a mode change reflects a transient period whereby the system is not fully delivering its functionality, it can be seen as an overhead that affects in an undesirable manner the performance of a real-time system. Therefore further work is necessary to address the issue of how to reduce the impact of a mode change upon the systems performance while still guaranteeing the schedulability requirements. From the discussions earlier, there is much work to do in formulating ways of reducing the worst case latency of a mode change. Since the latency of a mode change is a function of the offsets of new tasks and their worst case response times, we can investigate approaches of choosing appropriate values for the offsets in order to minimize the duration of a mode change. One possibility is to reduce the offset of each task but that would cause an increase on higher priority old mode tasks' interference up to a limit whereby deadlines start to be missed. Large values for all offsets clearly assure the schedulability of the tasks but may also dramatically increase the duration of a mode change. These and other related issues are subject of current work being undertaken by the authors.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Mode changes are acknowledgedly an important requirement in many applications involving real-time systems. They have been treated formerly in conventional systems as a part of cyclic executives. New scheduling techniques have been developed, and they correspondingly require new approaches for accomplishing mode changes. As flexible systems emerge in real-time applications, the way mode changes are viewed and implemented has to be made flexible as well. This work represents a first step to provide flexibility to mode changes in the new generation of flexible real-time systems.

As we pointed out in section 1, our main concern is to guarantee the schedulability of tasks that start in the old mode and run across the mode change period, and of tasks that are introduced during the mode change.

Although the proposed model is simple, the implications in the analysis and its benefits for the application are crucial. The analysis for the schedulability of tasks across a mode change becomes much simpler. It still provides a necessary and sufficient condition to the evaluation of the schedulability of tasks in a mode change. The application can benefit from the inherent advantages of the offset analysis during a mode change, while the whole approach to modelling mode changes becomes more realistic as the mode change process is treated as an interval of time instead of an instantaneous event.

The mode change analysis for old tasks (equations 8 and 9) keep the property of 'null mode change', the condition whereby all old mode versions are the same as their corresponding new mode versions (ie. 8 j : T j,1O = T jN ; C j,1O = C jN and x = 0). The analysis reduces to the original deadline monotonic analysis (given by equation 2) under these conditions.

This paper has introduced a new model for mode changes in flexible real-time systems. It has shown how the schedulability analysis for mode changes can benefit from having offsets and yet maintain full confidence that all timing requirements are satisfied.
